books.section: The Election of 1896 and the “Cross of Gold” Speech
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

stimulus.text: In 1896, William Jennings Bryan won the Democratic presidential nomination with his “Cross of Gold” speech calling for the free coinage of silver, and the People’s Party also nominated him. The Republican William McKinley, who stood for the gold standard, campaigned from his front porch in Canton, Ohio, receiving visitors instead of traveling. His campaign manager, Mark Hanna, raised far more money than Bryan’s campaign spent. McKinley won with 51 percent of the popular vote, and Republicans went on to dominate national politics for a generation. Every winner from 1876 through 1892 had taken less than half the popular vote. The last majority before 1896 was Grant’s in 1872.
stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of standard accounts, grounded in Barron’s Chapter 8, Topic 6.13, and 5 Steps Chapter 18.

stem: What does McKinley's 51 percent of the popular vote mark?

options.text: The first time a Democrat won the popular vote at all
options.misconception: Democrats had won the popular vote before, in 1876 and 1888.

options.text: The first time the electoral winner lost the popular vote
options.misconception: That had happened in 1876 and 1888; McKinley won both counts.

options.text: The first time a third party carried a whole region
options.misconception: Weaver carried states in 1892; McKinley's win is about a majority.

options.text: The first popular-vote majority in a presidential election since 1872

rationales.A: Tilden and Cleveland had won popular votes as Democrats before 1896.
rationales.B: McKinley won the electoral vote 271 to 176 as well as the popular vote.
rationales.C: Weaver carried western states in 1892, before McKinley's win.
rationales.D: No winner since Grant in 1872 had taken a majority; McKinley did.
rationales.general:
Put 51 percent beside the earlier winners.
1. McKinley took 51 percent of the popular vote in 1896.
2. Every winner from 1876 through 1892 had taken less than half.
3. A majority after twenty years of near-ties marks a break in the pattern.
4. The last majority before 1896 was Grant's in 1872.
Remember: a first in a long run of near-ties marks a turning point.
